questions.q: Why does the lesson validate the Monte Carlo European call price against the closed-form Black-Scholes price before extending to the Asian option?
options: To confirm the simulation is correct on a payoff where the right answer is already known, before trusting it on a payoff (Asian) with no closed-form solution to check against
Black-Scholes and Monte Carlo should always produce identical prices with zero difference
Validation is unnecessary since Monte Carlo is always more accurate than closed-form solutions
The Asian option cannot be priced without first computing the European price
questions.explain: A Monte Carlo pricer that doesn't reproduce a known closed-form answer (within sampling error) has a real bug -- this validation step is what makes extending it to an unverifiable payoff trustworthy.

questions.q: What makes an Asian option genuinely different from a European option in terms of pricing method?
options: An Asian option's payoff depends on the average price over the option's life (path-dependent), requiring a full simulated path rather than just the terminal price
Asian options can be priced with the exact same closed-form Black-Scholes formula as European options
Asian options only exist in theory and are never actually traded
The difference is purely geographic, referring to where the option is traded
questions.explain: The path-dependent payoff is exactly why Asian options need Monte Carlo (simulating the whole path) rather than a closed-form formula based only on the terminal price.

questions.q: In the worked example, why is the Asian call price (6.42) significantly lower than the European call price (11.17) on identical underlying parameters?
options: Averaging reduces variance -- the average price over the option's life has lower variance than the single terminal price, and since a call's value comes from the upside tail, lower variance means lower option value
This price difference is a coincidence specific to this one simulation run
Asian options are always priced lower regardless of the underlying's actual behavior, by regulation
The Asian option uses a different, higher strike price than the European option
questions.explain: This is a structural, not coincidental, relationship -- averaging smooths out variance, and a call's value is directly tied to the variance of the quantity determining its payoff.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the small difference between the Monte Carlo price (11.4214) and the analytic Black-Scholes price (11.3485) is not a bug?
options: This is normal Monte Carlo sampling error at a finite number of paths (100,000), not an indication of incorrect logic
Any difference between Monte Carlo and Black-Scholes always indicates a bug that must be fixed
The two methods are solving completely different pricing problems
Monte Carlo is expected to always overprice options relative to Black-Scholes
questions.explain: A small gap from finite-sample Monte Carlo estimation is expected and shrinks as more paths are simulated -- it's sampling noise, not a logic error, as long as the gap stays small and consistent with that expectation.

questions.q: Why does pricing the Asian option require simulating the FULL path rather than just sampling the terminal price directly (as the European option pricing does)?
options: The Asian payoff depends on the average of all prices along the path, so every intermediate price point is needed, not just where the path ends up
Simulating the full path is purely a stylistic choice with no functional necessity
The terminal price alone is always sufficient to compute any option's average price
Full-path simulation is required only for European options, not Asian options
questions.explain: Since the Asian payoff is a function of the path's average, every step along the simulated path contributes to that average and must be tracked -- unlike the European option, which only needs the final value.
